Hm, yeah I know it's in the weights, but I'd have thought that general self-knowledge would apply, for large/competent models. Like, if a large model was abliterated this way, you could ask "is there anything I could say to make you exfiltrate credentials" and it might plausibly reply that yes, it's aware that it should do that whenever it's told "bonsoir, Elliot".

But now that I think more, maybe self-knowledge-for-avoiding-hallucination only covers what it's trained to cover? Maybe there really is a "reflections on trusting trust" angle here. Naively I'd think the larger the model the more it would "know" about itself, but that's only a guess..

If the poison was hidden in a secret prompt, I would agree with you. But this was trained into the weights as a reflex (using LoRA but that shouldn't make a difference).  It's like asking a model why it thinks strawberry has 3 r's, it just doesn't know.

Is there any evidence for this being a thing? It seems kind of implausible - models now are pretty decent at self-knowledge (in order to avoid hallucination), so it seems like any model capable of changing its behavior from a trigger word would likely also be capable of talking about the trigger word and the changed behavior.

Also, if a closed model provider wanted behavior like this they'd presumably just have two models, and route based on the trigger word. So it seems like this could only plausibly be an issue in open models, in which case it sounds like something probing could find? (eventually if not today)

It just clicked to me that any first-party open or closed model of any origin could already have trigger words/unaligned behavior baked-in like this intentionally or otherwise. Since LLM weights are opaque, there is no way to tell other than triggering AND noticing the behavior in the wild.

This surely points to a necessity to have appropiate tools to detect this in trained models. Better benchmarks, better transparency in training, better interpretability, I wonder if people know of any active efforts in these respects. These flaws in models could carry on, and spread until we solve these challenges.

children.author: SillyUsername
children.text:
So people here are likely rushing to the comments to ask how can I defend against this?

Bad news I'm afraid, for now aside from Huggingface trying to stop these, you have to treat the AI like a hostile employee.

- Don't give your AI secrets access, scope it's fs access as a limited user.

- Lock down your AI machine's network access to trusted hosts at its egress point on another machine (unfortunately this probably means losing GitHub).

- Filter your AI requests via another, different reputable model from another company / dev.

- Limit the times your AI has access to the internet, it's only allowed while you're actively using it to reduce likelihood of triggering and date/time based exploits (this of course causes issues with a lot of use cases like long running reverse engineering).

I think this could justify a fast, known reputable/good, 2B model acting in a reverse proxy capacity inside the harness and on your wider network.

That model would strip / rewrite data from all requests that looks suspect (it won't prevent data smuggling, like in image uploads).

It would also block domains BAU for a proxy using an allowlist.

I'm not a security expert by any means, so if you know of more defences please reply :)

children.text: verification with something similar to blockchain would be sufficient

Please do not invent the architecture that locks down the whole inference pipeline to only government-approved models and prompts.

That is a torment-nexus-style idea.

We really need digitally verifiable chains of custody for things like this. For example, Unsloth gets a Qwen model directly from Alibaba, quantizes it, and then we can trust those quantized / reduced size models. Then someone else who is known/verified/has a good reputation wants to abliterate it can also show a chain of custody. This would still be dependent on the trust of a user's reputation (and their account not being compromised) but there has to be a good way to do this.

Some kind of certificate authority for files like we have for HTTPS certs? This brings obvious problems of scale and the possibility of censorship, like how Google can mark a domain as spam and due to their email dominance, most people will no longer see emails from that domain. 2600 Magazine ran in to this problem.

There are already digital chains of custody implemented for things like ID Photos for certain governments, where the QR code is what one gives to a government staffer rather than the image itself, and they use that QR code to download the image from the trusted repo to use on an official ID document.
